title: UK says it will monitor AI-based medical devices continually
source_used: Reuters (text read on a copy at Global Banking & Finance Review, Reuters byline Bhanvi Satija, dated Oct 6) and the official UK government release on gov.uk, published 6 Oct 2026
key_facts: On 6 Oct 2026 the UK government confirmed it will accept all 44 recommendations of the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare, whose report was published on 10 Sep 2026 (gov.uk); Reuters reports the same.

Lawrence Tallon, chief executive of the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA), told Reuters that AI-based medical devices will need constant monitoring after approval, rather than a single pre-approval safety check.
Tallon described a more sophisticated and complex era of AI as a medical device with non-deterministic algorithms, which Reuters explains as AI systems that evolve and adapt while doctors use them.

The Commission, an independent panel led by NHS doctors, concluded that AI-enabled medical devices should be assessed and monitored throughout their working life instead of relying on one-time assessments (gov.uk).

The MHRA committed to issue draft guidance by December 2026 on managing changes to AI-enabled devices as they adapt over time, and to begin consulting in 2027 on how to qualify and classify them (gov.uk).
A full implementation roadmap for all 44 recommendations is due by spring 2027 (gov.uk); Reuters says a draft plan is expected by the end of 2026.

The MHRA opened applications for phase 3 of AI Airlock, its regulatory sandbox for AI-enabled medical devices, focused on monitoring after devices are in use; the first innovators are to be selected in Nov 2026 (gov.uk).

Tallon told Reuters many nations are now approaching the UK to learn from its approach; the government is also exploring staged authorisation routes that let promising AI tools enter the NHS earlier under close supervision (gov.uk).
quote_evidence: AI-based medical devices will need constant monitoring even after they're approved for use, rather than a single pre-approval safety check, the head of the UK's medicines regulator said on Tuesday.
The UK government will accept all 44 recommendations from a report on how such AI tools are approved, it said.

One of the Commission’s central conclusions was that AI-enabled medical devices should be assessed and monitored throughout their working life to better understand true performance, instead of over-relying on one-time assessments.
why_it_matters_hint: AI medical devices in the UK are to be watched throughout their working life rather than approved once; the detailed guidance and the full plan are still to come.
notes: Reuters page returned HTTP 401. Reuters text read on a copy site (Global Banking & Finance Review) and checked against the official gov.uk release of 6 Oct 2026; the government release confirms every Reuters point used. The government's response answers the Commission's report of 10 Sep 2026 (named in the summary). Not repeated: the copy site's own headline 'Sets New Rules' (rules are not written yet) and its bullet that Britain is the first country with comprehensive rules (attribution unclear). The Scottish Government says it will set out its own response in due course.
